title: The medicine of immortality
hook: Ignatius calls the Eucharist the medicine of immortality and stresses unity with the bishop

segments.voice: Yesterday, Theophorus: Ignatius, the God-bearer, writing on his road to the beasts. Your line was wheat of God.

A bathroom cabinet is a small pharmacy: something for headaches, something for a cough, a half-finished prescription. Medicine is an ordinary thing to keep in a house. It's also an admission: bodies break, and everyone would like to put off the end a little longer. Ignatius, still on his road to Rome, reaches for exactly that ordinary word when he writes about the bread Christians share.
screen: `A CABINET OF MEDICINES.` → `BODIES BREAK.` → `IGNATIUS REACHES FOR THAT WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Writing to the Christians of Ephesus, Ignatius asks them to gather in one faith around their bishop and priests, breaking one bread, which he calls "the medicine of immortality": an antidote, he adds, so that we should not die but live forever in Jesus Christ. In Greek, pharmakon athanasias. The cure for death, handed out at a table. Second, where the picture comes from. In John's Gospel Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." Whoever eats this bread, he goes on, will live forever. Ignatius gives that hope a household name: medicine. Third, why the bishop comes into it. For Ignatius, the cure works in a body that holds together. To Philadelphia he writes: take care to keep one Eucharist, for there is one flesh of our Lord, one cup, one altar, as there is one bishop. To Smyrna he says the Eucharist should be the one celebrated with the bishop, or someone he appoints. Earlier in the letter to Ephesus, he calls Christ the one physician. Fourth, how it's read today. Catholics, and Orthodox Christians too, read Ignatius as an early witness to what they believe: that the Eucharist is truly the body and blood of Christ, celebrated in communion with the bishop. In the letter to Smyrna he mentions people who stayed away from the Eucharist because they did not confess it to be the flesh of Christ. Some Protestant readers treasure his letters while reading these lines in their own way. At every Catholic Mass, the local bishop is still named aloud in the Eucharistic Prayer, right in the middle of the bread and the cup. One bread, one bishop, said at once.
screen: `PHARMAKON ATHANASIAS.` · `THE LIVING BREAD.` · `ONE CUP, ONE ALTAR, ONE BISHOP.` · `NAMED AT EVERY MASS.` · then, large: `THE MEDICINE OF IMMORTALITY.`

segments.voice: If you're Catholic and know your bishop's name, hold it in mind, or listen for it in the Eucharistic Prayer next time you're at Mass; on another path, think of whoever holds your community together, a pastor, a principal, a parent. Picture them on a hard day, with everyone's complaints on their desk. If you pray, ask wisdom and strength for them; if you don't, wish them well, plainly.
pharmakon athanasias. Ignatius's Greek name for the Eucharist: the medicine of immortality, the one bread that keeps a church whole. Today's word.
Your line: one bread, one bishop. A medicine meant for one table. Day seven hundred four, done.

howItsDone: At every Catholic Mass the local bishop is named in the Eucharistic Prayer, and Catholics receive Communion as the body and blood of Christ, in communion with their bishop and the pope.

chat.says: Why would Ignatius call the Eucharist a medicine?
options: He saw the one bread as an antidote to death, so people might live forever in Christ.
Early Christians took the bread to cure fevers and other illnesses of the body.
He meant it tasted bitter like medicine, a penance to swallow, not a gift.
chat.meaning: Ignatius calls the one bread the medicine of immortality, an antidote so that believers should not die but live forever in Jesus Christ.

notes: John 6 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording and verse number (Douay numbers John 6 one verse differently in places): confirm.
'the medicine of immortality' attributed to Lightfoot's translation of Ephesians 20: confirm. The rest of Ephesians 20 ('the antidote that we should not die') is paraphrased.
The statement of Catholic and Orthodox belief and the line 'Many Protestant Christians treasure his letters while reading these lines in their own way' should be checked for fairness by the Keeper.
'The bishop of the place is still named aloud in the Eucharistic Prayer' at every Mass: confirm wording (diocesan bishop named; pope named too).
Ignatius letters are paraphrased except the short phrase quoted; Keeper may prefer exact Lightfoot quotations throughout.

Audit: 'Ignatius takes that promise' asserted that he drew on John 6, which scholars debate, so it now says he gives 'that same hope' a name; the 'patient refusing the medicine' analogy was put in Ignatius's mouth without a source and is replaced by his own 'one physician' (Ephesians 7). Confirm.
